newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK government seen seeking to cool property boom.
newsitem.headline: HK government seen seeking to cool property boom.

text.p: Hong Kong's spiralling property prices are raising expectations that the government will attempt to cool speculative buying, analysts said on Thursday.
"Property prices have essentially gone to a level which is affecting the economic well being of the general public," said Benjamin Cheng, executive director at Goldman Sachs.
"No one will want to kill the market -- our economic well being depends on property prices -- but investors never cool down by themselves," he said.
Legislators, consumer and business lobbies have all voiced concerns over a rise of some 20-30 percent in residential property prices in 1996.

Prices have continued rising this year and show no sign of flattening out as the rush for Sun Hung Kai Properties Ltd's latest flats illustrates. Prices for its development in the Tseung Kwan O new town in the New Territories rose nine percent in under a week to HK$5,214 per square foot from $4,771.
"I think the fact that we have seen so many registrations for this project shows there is definitely speculation," said Martin Tacon, senior associate at CS First Boston.
He expects the government to respond swiftly.
"They are going to have to make a decision on whether they are going to intervene and they are going to have to make a decision within the next three days," he said.
Hong Kong shares took a beating on Thursday as anticipation of government measures sent property stocks into a tailspin. The Hang Seng index slumped 1.91 percent to 13,198.11 points.
Hong Kong's Consumer Council said it is studying possible measures to cool down the market and the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce has also urged the government to act soon.
Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten said on Wednesday the government was concerned about the anxieties being expressed.

"The sorts of things they might do to curb demand is simply to put a bit of pressure on banks to curb liquidity in the mortgage market and also put pressure on the major developers," said Peter Churchouse, regional strategist at Morgan Stanley.
Tacon said the mostly likely form of intervention would probably take the form of limiting the number of flats in a development sold to companies.
Sun Hung Kai Properties ensured companies could take no more than 20 percent of the flats offered in Tseung Kwan O.

"They (the government) may introduce a compulsory restriction on the percentage that can be bought by companies and that could well be below the 20 percent mark that Sun Hung Kai has voluntarily put in place or it might put a complete ban on companies buying flats below a certain price level," said Tacon.
Local newspapers reported on Thursday that more than 27,000 potential buyers had registered for the sale at the Tseung Kwan O development.

At a luxury apartment development in Kowloon this week, one buyer paid HK$2 million for the right to be among the first in line to buy one of the 76 flats on offer, beating $1.3 million paid at the release of another luxury development recently.

Analysts said the long-term solution was not to quell demand but increase supply. "The main remedy lies in making more land available for all types of residential property and this should be announced as quickly as possible," said Ian Christie, director of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce.
